abstract.p: Scaling approaches are used to describe or predict clearance for paediatric or obese populations from normal-weight adult values. Theoretical allometry assumes the existence of a universal bodyweight-based scaling relationship. Although theoretical allometry is highly disputed, it is commonly applied in pharmacological data analyses and clinical practice. The aim of the current review is to (1) increase pharmacologists’ understanding of theoretical allometry to better understand the (implicit) assumptions and (dis)advantages and (2) highlight important methodological considerations with the application of this methodology. Theoretical allometry originated in an empirical, and later debated, observation by Kleiber of a scaling exponent of 0.75 between basal metabolic rate and body mass of mammals. The mathematical framework of West, Brown, and Enquist provides one possible explanation for this value. To date, multiple key assumptions of this framework have been disputed or disproven, and an increasing body of evidence is emerging against the existence of one universal allometric exponent. The promise of ease and universality of use that comes with theoretical approaches may be the reason they are so strongly sought after and defended. However, ecologists have suggested that the theory should move from a ‘Newtonian approach’, in which physical explanations are sought for a universal law and variability is of minor importance, to a ‘Darwinian approach’, in which variability is considered of primary importance for which evolutionary explanations can be found. No scientific support was found for the application of allometry for within-species scaling, so the application of basal metabolic rate-based scaling principles to clearance scaling remains unsubstantiated. Recent insights from physiologically based modelling approaches emphasise the interplay between drugs with different properties and physiological variables that underlie drug clearance, which drives the variability in the allometric scaling exponent in the field of pharmacology. To deal with this variability, drug-specific or patient-specific adaptations to theoretical allometric scaling are proposed, that introduce empiric elements and reduce the universality of the theory. The use of allometric scaling with an exponent of 0.75 may hold empirical merit for paediatric populations, except for the youngest individuals (aged ≤ 5 years). Nevertheless, biological interpretations and extrapolation potential attributed to models based on 0.75 allometric scaling are theoretically unfounded, and merits of the empirical application of this function should, as for all models, always be supported by appropriate model validation procedures. In this respect, it is not the value of the allometric exponent but the description and prediction of individual clearance values and drug concentrations that are of primary interest.

sec.title: Key Points

tr.td: Theoretical allometry is commonly applied in pharmacological data analysis, but a substantial amount of both theoretical and empirical evidence against the theory from the field of ecology makes it unsuited to theoretically inform pharmacological models.
A single, universal allometric exponent is unlikely to exist and is instead expected to vary based on many factors such as drug properties and physiological characteristics such as age and weight.
Application of theoretical allometry for paediatric pharmacology holds empirical merit down to children aged 5 years, provided the developed model is appropriately validated.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Can drug clearance (CL), the driver of steady state and trough concentrations, derived from normal-weight adults be used to inform drug dosing in special populations, such as paediatric or obese populations? This question has been subject to fierce debate within the field of pharmacology. As CL is often correlated with bodyweight, the characterisation of this correlation is of great scientific interest. Estimation of parameters describing this relationship requires informative data, but theoretical guidelines are sought that can be used in the absence of sufficiently informative data. This would, for example, prove useful in the selection of a dose for a first-in-child study or when determining a dosing regimen for an individual with obesity when information on this is lacking. One proposed theory for this is fixed 0.75 allometric scaling (AS0.75), which defines CL to scale with bodyweight with a universal scaling exponent of 0.75 [1]. Although many pharmacologists might recognise this theoretical relationship as proprietary to their field, its origins can be traced back to ecology.

Allometry refers to the study of (non-linear) relationships between bodyweight and anatomical features or physiological processes. Within ecology, the relationship between bodyweight and basal metabolic rate (BMR, i.e., the energy expenditure at rest) has been of great interest. Although originally applied to between-species BMR scaling, allometric scaling with an exponent of 0.75 has also been extrapolated to scaling within species. Additionally, in pharmacology, it has been taken one step further by applying principles of BMR to CL. Because of its simplicity and the existence of a theoretical explanation, AS0.75 gained widespread popularity, but remains highly debated in both pharmacology and ecology. However, a clear overview of all aspects of its theoretical basis and application in pharmacology is lacking, which makes it difficult for pharmacologists to grasp the discussion in its entirety and to make a well-informed decision on its application. Therefore, the aim of this review is to introduce pharmacologists to the theoretical background of AS0.75, as well as to the theoretical and empirical arguments in favour and against it. We provide practical considerations to the application of this approach in human pharmacology, with particular focus on paediatric and obese populations.

sec.title: The origin of Allometric Scaling
3/4 Power Scaling for Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)
sec.p: Scientists as far back as Galileo have been mystified by the relationship between the rate of physiological processes and the bodyweight of species [2]. Mathematically, the simplest relationship is a linear one. When applied to pharmacology, this would mean that the dose for a child of 10 kg would be one-seventh of the adult dose (assuming an average adult bodyweight of 70 kg). This was already shown in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries to lead to underdosing in children [3]. Non-linear relationships therefore seemed more adequate to capture the relationship between bodyweight and physiology.

The first widely adopted non-linear allometric relationship was proposed in 1838, when an animal’s BMR was found to be directly proportional to its body surface area [4]. As body surface area ∝ bodyweight2/3, it followed that BMR ∝ bodyweight2/3. Although empirical in nature, this is known as the surface area law. The surface area law has not remained free of criticism, as multiple assumptions are challenged, for instance, the assumption that the radiating capacity of animals is equal between species or that temperature of the skin is constant and equal for the entire body [5, 6]. In 1932, Max Kleiber empirically investigated the relationship between BMR and bodyweight of mammals spanning a larger bodyweight range and found an allometric scaling exponent (b) of 3/4 [7]. This empiric relationship has become known as Kleiber’s law.
where BW is the bodyweight of the species, a is an empiric coefficient, and b is the allometric scaling exponent.

sec.title: West, Brown, and Enquist’s Theoretical Framework for 3/4 Power Scaling of Basal Metabolic Rate Between Species
sec.p: Many studies sought to provide theoretical support for Kleiber’s empirically derived allometric exponent of 3/4, with the most influential being the mathematical framework by West, Brown, and Enquist (WBE) [13–15].

Central to the WBE framework, is that “Living things are sustained by the transport of materials through linear networks that branch to supply all parts of the organism” [14]. These transport systems are assumed to be of a fractal nature and to fill the entire volume of an organism. Two other essential assumptions are that the final branch of the fractal system is size invariant (i.e., independent of the animal’s size) and that energy minimisation (i.e., minimisation of the energy required for optimal flow through the network) is the driving force within the fractal network. For a complete mathematical derivation, the reader is directed to the original article [14]; here, we highlight the main aspects required to understand how WBE derived that b from Eq. 1 must be 3/4.

WBE use analogies to the vascular system to illustrate the theoretical concepts, for example, ‘flow’ through ‘networks’ is represented as blood flow through the vascular system (Fig. 2). The vascular system starts at the aorta and branches out until terminating at the capillaries (c). WBE define the aorta as level k = 0, which branches down in N branches. Any given branch at level k has a length (lk), radius (rk), and drop in pressure (Δpk). Each vessel branches into nk daughter branches. Blood flow (Q) in the aorta (Qo) is conserved throughout the system, so that Q0 = NkQk = NcQc. Because all nutrients required to sustain a BMR are transported via this flow, it follows that Qo ∝ BMR. Accepting the previously defined proportionality of BMR ∝ Mb, it must follow that Q0 ∝ Mb, with M referring to body mass. Moreover, as the total amount of capillaries (Nc) serve as the final supplier of nutrients for metabolic processes, Nc ∝ BMR and therefore it must follow that Nc ∝ Mb.Fig. 2
Visualisation of the concepts and parameters used in the framework of West, Brown, and Enquist. Shown are a side view (top) and cross-sectional view (bottom) of the vascular system, which branches from the aorta (left) to the capillaries (right)

Second, the authors propose that the branching of consecutive levels of vessels can be characterised with scaling factors for the radius (r) and length (l). These scaling factors are the ratio between the radius or length of a level k + 1 and level k and are denoted β and γ, respectively. Because of the assumptions of self-similarity of the network and energy minimisation in the system, n, β and γ are independent of k.

Here, M0 is defined as a “normalisation scale for M”, for which the precise definition remains unclear but, in a footnote, WBE mention that “normalisation factors, such as M0, will generally be suppressed.”

Of note is that the provided derivation is based on non-pulsatile systems. For pulsatile systems such as the mammalian vascular system, more mathematically intense and elaborate theoretical considerations are discussed, for which the reader is directed to the original publication by WBE [14]. Ultimately, this also yields b = 3/4.

sec.title: Heated Discussions on WBE’s Framework
sec.p:
The theoretical framework by WBE to support Kleiber’s observation caused a resurgence of the interest in allometric scaling but also sparked a major debate. Other papers building on the concept of the fractal nature of biology, as well as empirical studies in favour of 3/4 scaling over 2/3 scaling, were published in the context of BMR [16, 17] but also to explain mitochondrial aerobic metabolism [18], plant growth [19, 20], rates of population growth [21, 22], and more [17, 23, 24], with all publications co-authored by one of the original WBE authors. However, others pointed out that the WBE framework was developed to explain but not predict an empirically derived exponent of 3/4 and as such provides one possible explanation but not conceptual proof. For instance, in 2016, Kwak et al. provided a theoretical framework to explain 2/3 scaling [25]. In addition to this, other topics remain on which consensus between proponents and opponents of the framework has not been reached. sec.title: Theoretical Critiques on the WBE Framework
Service Volumes
sec.p: In 2004, Kozłowsky and Konarzewski (K&K) published a paper in which they stated that “WBE’s model is mathematically incorrect” [26]. According to these authors, this bold statement follows from the definition of the service volume. An important assumption of WBE states that the capillaries are size invariant. The capillaries supply a service volume with a diameter of the length of a capillary (lc). K&K subsequently argue that, because lc is size invariant, the number of capillaries (Nc) must be directly proportional to the total body volume (W), which is directly proportional to body mass (M). So, if M ∝ W and W ∝ 4/3π(lc/2)3Nc, from the size invariance of lc, it must follow that Nc ∝ M and not Nc ∝ M3/4. K&K therefore conclude that either b must be equal to 1 or the assumption on the size invariance of lc must be violated. K&K continue by showing that, aside from this theoretical inconsistency, the derivation of b = 3/4 is incorrect. WBE make use of the relation (γβ2)−N ∝ M, which itself is based on the proportionality of total blood volume (Vb) and mass, Vb ∝ M. K&K state that, according to capillary size invariance, the blood volume present within capillaries, which is VcNc, must be proportional to M, not total blood volume Vb as suggested by WBE. Vb should increase supralinearly with M, as more fluid is present within vessels not supplying any tissues. In that case and based on numerical examples, K&K state that (γβ2)−N ∝ M4/3 and not (γβ2)−N ∝ M as proposed by WBE. Overall, the derivation of b = 3/4 based on the erroneous (γβ2)−N ∝ M therefore does not hold in their opinion.

Hereafter, we refer to WBE’s response to K&K as WBE2005 and statements from the original publication as WBE1997. In WBE2005, the authors claim that “[K&K] misread our paper, misrepresented our model, and made serious mistakes” [27]. They state that K&K interpreted the size invariance described in WBE1997 to imply that a constant volume of tissue will be supplied by a capillary [26, 27]. However, WBE2005 indicate that, in their framework, the service volume scales to body size via the relationship M1/4. According to WBE2005, K&K take size invariance to mean that Nc must scale isometrically with bodyweight. However, WBE2005 argue that the size invariance of the capillaries and the way that Nc scales are independent. Quickly after, K&K responded [28], saying WBE did not manage to accurately refute their critique and that, unless b is equal to one, a logical fallacy remains within their framework. They restate that Nc ∝ Mb (as stated in WBE1997) is needed to satisfy Qo ∝ BMR. However, Nc ∝ M1 is required to allow size invariant service volumes. According to K&K, this fundamental inconsistency can only be solved in one of three ways: (1) assuming density of tissues increases with body mass with an exponent of 1 − b (which K&K deem unlikely), (2) giving up the assumption of capillary size invariance, or (3) assuming b = 1. K&K note that solution (2) is the only one supported by empirical evidence [29–31]. Overall, the two sides remain unreconciled. The discussion illustrates the complexity of the assumptions introduced by WBE, and the difficulty in their interpretation.

Etienne et al. tried to offer a solution to the impasse [32]. According to these authors, the disagreement is caused by how a space-filling network is interpreted. WBE interpret this as a preservation of 4/3π(lk/2)3Nk for every level k, simplified to Nklk3 for ease of reading. According to Etienne et al., WBE assume Nklk3 to be proportional to the service volume of all vessels. WBE treat the assumption of a space-filling fractal such that the entire volume of an organism is filled with service volumes. This is also corroborated by others: “[…] network extent and structure must be such that its terminal points can service (and thus cover) the entire body volume” [33]. However, Etienne et al. argue that, if the service volume is proportional to Nclc3 and this volume fills the entire body, it will scale with body size as 4/3π(lk/2)3Nk ∝ M, as concluded by K&K. The solution to this is to forgo the assumption that 4/3π(lk/2)3Nk corresponds to the entire body volume and adopt the assumption that the quantity 4/3π(lk/2)3Nk is preserved through all levels k. The extent to which this resolves the discussion on size invariance of capillaries and service volumes is questionable, as the main concern K&K posed was related to the incompatibility of size invariance of capillaries with the service volumes, not the relationship between service volumes and total body volume itself.

sec.title: Biological Relevance and Universality of the WBE Framework
sec.p: WBE present their framework to apply to a wide range of supply networks, including mammalian vasculature and respiratory systems, plant vascular systems, and tracheal tubes of insects [14]. However, K&K point out that assumptions by WBE on branching of supply vessels do not take the organism’s geometry into account [26]. For instance, for mammalian vasculature, this implies that vessels running from the heart to abdominal organs would split similarly to those running to limb extremities, the reality of which K&K question. The mesh-like organisation of capillaries is also not represented by the hierarchical branching presented in WBE. Additionally, K&K note that WBE’s assumptions do not consider differences in tissue perfusion in mammals [26]. As not all capillaries can be completely filled at the same time, because of a lack of blood to do so, K&K argue that the supplying system adjusts to cover tissue demand, rather than the supplying system limiting BMR. This explains why an animal’s metabolism increases when they become active, which would not be possible if the delivery of nutrients was rate limiting at rest. Time-varying energy consumption by organs and acclimatisation to different climates can also lead to physiological differences in tissue perfusion, therefore one can question whether the assumption of one capillary exclusively servicing one service volume is always correct. Finally, K&K highlight that the assumption by WBE of a constant number of daughter branches at each node of the network is violated by empirical findings that, depending on the intensity of metabolism, the proportion of capillaries opened to blood flow varies [28].

Regarding plant vasculature and tracheal systems of insects, K&K have raised further questions on the biological validity of assumptions in those specific contexts, disputing the proposed universality of the WBE framework. Arguments on these topics have been going back and forth [27, 28], but also here the different authors do not settle their disputes. Others have also critiqued the application of the WBE framework to plants, concluding that the framework is too simplistic to apply to vascular plants and critique it for not taking important ontogenetic changes into account [34].

sec.title: Mathematical Critiques
sec.p: Aside from K&K, others have raised doubts about the mathematical validity of the WBE framework. Dodds et al. have analysed theoretical derivations of the 3/4 power scaling law [35] and assessed the assumption made by WBE that the networks are fractal in nature. In WBE1997, the network impedance (or resistance, Z) of pulsatile systems is minimised via a so-called Lagrange multiplier method. The fractal nature of the system is partly described via this minimisation procedure. However, Dodds et al. show that Z indeed is minimised when γk = βk = nk−1/3, but their calculations show it is not necessarily level independent and therefore does not prove that the network must necessarily be fractal.

Chaui-Berlinck thoroughly assesses the mathematical support for the assumptions made by WBE1997 in a pulsatile system [36]. WBE show that β = n−1/2 in non-pulsatile systems, which is essential to be able to derive that b = 3/4. However, Chaui-Berlinck illustrates that this pivotal relationship is not proven in a pulsatile system and that derivations of this relationship are not in line with empirical findings. Chaui-Berlinck also concludes that the relationship of Vb ∝ M has never been proven and investigates this assumption in a pulsatile system by considering energy minimisation to conclude that “WBE cannot prove their claim that a linear relationship between fluid volume and body mass is a natural consequence of geometric/impedance constraints in living beings”. Lastly, Chaui-Berlinck argues, like K&K, but through different reasoning, that, because the service volume is calculated as 4/3π(lc/2)3 and the capillaries have an invariant length, the service volumes must also be an invariant unit, meaning the relationship Nc ∝ Mb can only be true if b = 1. Much like the critique by K&K, the report by Chaui-Berlinck sparked a discussion between the author and WBE [37, 38], in which the authors do not reconcile their differing views.

In a reanalysis of two theoretical frameworks, including the WBE framework, that aim to explain b = 3/4, Makarieva et al. discuss the implications of the assumed proportionality Vb ∝ M. They find that the framework would only yield B ∝ M3/4 if M ∝ l04, with l0 being the linear size of the total volume of the fractal network [39]. A common assumption would be l0 ∝ L (body length), as in the framework by Banavar et al. [15], which also aims to a theoretical explanation for b = 3/4. This is deemed problematic because empirical observations show M ∝ L3 in mammals. However, WBE circumvent this problem by introducing l0 as independent from L. But, as noted by Makarieva et al., this creates the inherent problem that the network must stretch along the whole body (L) to supply all parts of the organism, instead of being restricted to its own spatial scale l0. This yields two linear scales within one organism, which is shown by Makarieva et al. to not be supported by empirical evidence. They show that the assumption Vb ∝ M causes the WBE framework to predict the length of the aorta to scale with M1/4, whereas available evidence shows it to scale as M1/3. Also shown is that the assumption of M ∝ l04, which is required if Vb ∝ M, would lead to the spatial volume of the network becoming increasingly large with smaller body sizes, even giving rise to volumes of the system larger than the body volume itself [39]. They conclude that “the WBE model cannot account for the scaling exponents in animals remaining simultaneously within the domains of biological and physical plausibility and mathematical coherence.”

Self-similar properties of biological transport systems have also been questioned on biological grounds by K&K. In response, Etienne et al. found that a scaling exponent of 3/4 can be derived without the assumption of self-similarity in the fractal networks [32]. However, their redefined WBE framework becomes even more theoretical in nature, including the introduction of topological quantities that “will be helpful in our derivation”, but for which it remains unclear what biological features they represent. As such, it is difficult to scrutinise the biological implications.

Apol et al. reanalysed WBE and critically discussed five assumptions. One critique is that energy dissipation has only been partially minimised by WBE. They show with further optimisations that the optimal branching ratio is 1, meaning that the optimal network predicted by the WBE framework is one large vessel that runs through the organism [40]. The scaling exponent would then be 0. By relaxing some of WBE’s assumptions, the framework predicts isometric scaling of BMR with body mass (i.e., b = 1), which they recognise to be incompatible with observed scaling exponents. They conclude that the WBE framework is not suited to ‘explain’ Kleiber’s law and suggest the reason for it may have to be sought outside of the realm of flow-limited network theory.

Finally, Savage, Deeds, and Fontana performed a thorough reanalysis of the WBE framework and a re-examination of the assumptions. They investigated network size, branching numbers, and when pulsatile flow (area-preserving branching) switches to smooth flow (area-increasing branching) and delineate how these aspects influence the scaling exponent [33]. Their main conclusion is that the 3/4 exponent derived by WBE only holds if the limits of mass, network size, and metabolic rate are approached. After finite-size corrections, a scaling exponent of 0.81 is predicted by the WBE framework.

sec.title: Empirical Findings to Disprove Kleiber’s Law and the WBE Framework
sec.p: In addition to theoretical discussions, empirical evidence to accept or reject Kleiber’s law and the WBE framework has also been reported. In 1982, Heusner concluded Kleiber’s law to be a statistical artefact and challenged both the derived allometric exponent of 3/4 and the assumed constancy of the mass coefficient (a in Eq. 1). He found the allometric exponent to be 2/3 for seven different species and the mass coefficient (a) to change with body mass and between species [9]. As such, Heusner concluded large and small mammals to lie on parallel regression lines with a slope of 2/3 [10].

In a thorough reanalysis of multiple datasets, including Kleiber’s original dataset, Dodds et al. found little statistical evidence to reject the 2/3 scaling law in favour of the 3/4 law [35]. Furthermore, they were unable to statistically reject 2/3 as the scaling exponent for mammals with a bodyweight smaller than 10 kg and for birds. For larger mammals, deviations from 2/3 were more common, but little evidence exists for accepting 3/4 over 2/3 as an allometric exponent.

White et al. [8] argue that Kleiber and others used datasets that unfairly represent species. For example, Artiodactyla are overrepresented, which, because of their relatively large weight, can lead to an overestimated exponent. They also argue that differences in body temperature between species should be acknowledged. Taking these considerations into account, their analysis of the correlation between bodyweight and BMR in 619 species from 19 mammalian orders yielded an estimated exponent of 2/3.

Hayssen and Lacy also critique Kleiber’s dataset, as they find it too small and unrepresentative of mammals, with 9 of 12 included species being domestic populations that do not live under natural conditions [41].

sec.title: Lack of Universality of the Allometric Exponent for Basal Metabolic Rate
sec.p: Although numerous discussions focused on whether 2/3 or 3/4 should be accepted as the universal scaling exponent, many have challenged the existence of a universal relationship altogether. For example, Hayssen and Lacy were unable to identify a single allometric exponent to describe the relationship of BMR and body mass in mammals [41]. White et al. published a meta-analysis on 127 allometric exponents for scaling BMR and found high heterogeneity of the exponent, suggesting that a universal scaling exponent does not exist [42], whereas Bokma’s scaling of BMR in fish indicated the same even for within-species scaling [43]. Heusner’s scaling of BMR within dogs resulted in a scaling exponent of 0.885, further refuting the (within-species) universality of 3/4 or 2/3 [44]. Clarke et al. found that the allometric exponent of species with a lower bodyweight was 2/3 and that it moved asymptotically to a value of around 3/4 with increasing bodyweight [45], which is in line with the results reported by Dodds et al. [35] and McNab et al. [46]. A dependency of the scaling exponent on bodyweight was also highlighted by Heusner [44] and reported by Lovegrove across 487 mammalian species [47]. Numerous other papers have proposed species characteristics that show correlations with the allometric scaling exponent for BMR, including taxonomical class or phylogenetics [48, 49], physical constraints of an organism [50, 51], zoogeographical zones, whether a species is a predator or not, and the mobility of animals [47]. In a series of papers, Kosłowski proposes how evolutionary principles can drive variability in the allometric exponent [52, 53]. In line with this view, in a recent review on the variability of allometric scaling exponents, Glazier shows the wide range of exponents that have been reported within different taxa [54]. They indicate a switch from a ‘Newtonian approach’ to allometric theory, in which physical explanations are sought for a universal law and variability is of minor importance, to a ‘Darwinian approach’, in which variability is considered of primary importance and for which evolutionary explanations can be found. As such, a shift can be seen in allometric theory no longer aiming to find physical explanations for a universal scaling law but instead explaining the variable nature of the allometric exponent due to “adaptable phenotypic plasticity and genotypic evolution,” which are impacted by biological and ecological influences [54].

sec.title: Conclusions for Pharmacologists
sec.p: The background of allometric theory is vast and has been summarised here to provide pharmacologists with the highlights of the efforts to concretise Kleiber’s empirical observations into mathematically based theories and of the theoretical and empirical discourse surrounding these theories. Readers interested in obtaining a more substantial understanding of this field are encouraged to read the extraordinarily in-depth reviews by Gould [55] and Glazier [56].

Although widely accepted and applied, Kleiber’s so-called law is highly debated. Empirical evidence exists to support both 3/4 and other allometric exponents, including 1 and 2/3, whereas some dispute the existence of a single exponent for all species altogether. The WBE theoretical framework is often claimed to provide a “strong theoretical basis” for AS0.75, whereas it is in fact surrounded by unsettled disputes and controversy.

For theoretical frameworks that bridge disciplines, in this case evolutionary biology and mathematics, it is important to ensure that all proposed arguments and assumptions are in line with the views of the respective fields. This makes it challenging to develop a theoretical framework and for individuals with limited knowledge on at least one of the respective fields to fully assess its credibility. This may partly explain the unresolved nature of discussions surrounding the framework by WBE. However, from Table 1, it becomes clear that this framework is highly dependent on multiple assumptions, with one or more counterarguments or alternative interpretations being available for a number of them. Unfortunately, experimental methods to investigate the assumptions under discussion are, in some cases, lacking. Finally, it should be remembered that the framework by WBE offers one possible explanation for an allometric scaling exponent of 3/4, which is not the same as proving that this has to be the case, and theories to support other exponents have also been proposed [25, 52, 53]. Therefore, although a universal scaling law as proposed by Kleiber and shaped by WBE appears appealing, many indicate that it might be an outdated view of the underlying nature of allometric relationships.

sec.title: Fixed 0.75 Allometric Scaling for Drug Clearance
sec.p:
Despite the disputes, Kleiber’s law has gained popularity in other scientific fields, including pharmacokinetics, as illustrated by the increase in the number of research publications on allometric principles in Fig. 3. To substantiate the use of Kleiber’s law in the context of human pharmacology, where it is mostly used to scale CL between (sub)populations, three assumptions are (implicitly) made, as illustrated in Fig. 4 (left panel), of which the first two have been discussed above and the third is discussed below.Fig. 3

Application of theoretical allometry in human pharmacology can be visualised as a temple (left). It is founded on two principles: Kleiber’s observational ‘law’ and the framework of West, Brown, and Enquist (WBE) for scaling of basal metabolic rate (BMR). Additionally, three assumptions are required to support the use of theoretical allometry (AS0.75) within human pharmacology. In reality, the basis of the temple is poorly supported, and the assumptions are shown to generally not hold (right). CL clearance

In the field of pharmacology, Holford et al. have stated that “It is a natural extension to assume that these theory-based allometric relationships developed for metabolic rate would also be appropriate for drug elimination processes that determine drug CL” [57]. Through this statement, a similarity between CL and metabolic processes at rest is claimed, although how “natural” this assertion is can be queried. The link between BMR that occurs in every cell of the body, and CL, the result of processes that are limited to specific organs only, is not obvious, particularly in view of the underlying assumptions by WBE1997 (Table 1). It is also implied that, because WBE theory explains an allometric exponent of 3/4 for metabolic processes, CL must follow the same principle, yet the veracity of this claim has been questioned [58] and never been proven.

Regarding between-species scaling of CL, empirical investigations on the suitability of AS0.75 have been carried out. Glomerular filtration rate, one of the driving forces for renal CL, was found to allometrically scale between species with an exponent of 3/4 [59, 60]; however, reports on other drugs, including hepatically metabolised drugs, derive a range of other values [61–63]. The largest comparative study, on 85 drugs, found the allometric exponent for inter-species scaling of CL to vary between drugs, being normally distributed with a mean of 0.87 [64]. Despite the weak theoretical basis and contradictory empirical evidence, the use of an allometric exponent of 0.75 for inter-species scaling of CL has gained traction, in both veterinarian practice and (pre)clinical drug development.

In publications applying CL scaling, different quantifications can be applied. In the work presented here, we refer to CL quantified as volume/time (e.g., L/min). When weight-normalised quantifications are used (e.g., L/min/kg or L/min/kg0.75), this will be explicitly defined. Moreover, although publications start to emerge on the applicability of AS0.75 for large molecules [65], it must be noted that, although there is also evidence for large molecules, most literature addresses AS0.75 in the context of small-molecule drugs.

sec.title: AS0.75 in Human Pharmacology
sec.p: A systematic review of 487 published population pharmacokinetic models, including humans of any age, revealed that 29.4% of all models included a non-linear relationship between CL and bodyweight and that 26.4% of these models relied on AS0.75 [66]. It was noted that the latter was especially predominant in studies in children and neonates. This shows that, after accepting AS0.75 for inter-species scaling of drug CL, it has also become popular to scale CL within species.

Where CLi is the scaled CL of individual i with weight Wi, and CLSTD is the typical CL of an individual with a standard weight WSTD. In humans, the standard weight is set to the weight of a normal-weight adult, for which 70 kg is generally used [67, 68].

In humans, AS0.75 is used in two scenarios: (1) to predict CL based on CL in a reference population (e.g., when no pharmacokinetic data are available in the population of interest) or (2) to describe inter-individual variability in CL in the analysis of available data. A reported justification for the latter is that AS0.75 captures “well-defined biological laws,” for which the work of WBE is then referenced and that AS0.75 therefore adds biologically relevant information to a model [67], whereas others claim AS0.75 to be unjustified because of the large amount of evidence against its theoretical basis [58, 69]. Another argument to support AS0.75 is that, compared with situations where different parameterisations and normalisations are used, the estimated CLSTD can be more easily compared between studies, (sub)populations, and drugs [68, 70], although any other normalisation would achieve the same purpose.

In children, age can also be quantified using other descriptors such as postnatal age (PNA) and gestational age. It has been argued that the use of PMA is most physiologically justified, as maturation of enzymes in the liver starts before birth [1, 91]. PMA has also been used to account for maturation of glomerular filtration rate when scaling CL of renally cleared drugs such as amikacin via AS0.75 [92–94]. However, evidence exists for differential prenatal and postnatal development of elimination routes, which would require functions that take a combination of PNA and gestational age into account [95]. Either way, the introduction of the maturation function as an empiric element comes with the requirement of data, which limits this application of AS0.75 with a maturation function to scenarios with informative data only.

sec.title: Theoretical Critiques on AS0.75 with a Maturation Function
sec.p: The use of an AS0.75 together with a maturation function is reported to allow for the disentanglement of the highly correlated covariates age and bodyweight in the paediatric population [67, 96, 97]. But, because age and bodyweight are so strongly correlated in (young) children, opponents argue that separation of the two is impossible. As such, introduction of bodyweight as a covariate with AS0.75 will also partly describe the influence of age, because of its correlation with bodyweight, leaving the maturation function to describe the mathematical residue that remains after the inclusion of the AS0.75 function, rather than being an actual quantification of maturation [69, 98].

Using a physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling approach, Calvier et al. tested the claim that AS0.75 accurately accounts for the size-related differences in paediatric CL [99] and showed that this claim is unsubstantiated. More specifically, through simulations with a paediatric PBPK model that only included equations for size-related changes in physiological parameters and that excluded all functions for maturational changes, they predicted adult and paediatric CL values for a wide range of hypothetical drugs. They then assessed how well the simulated paediatric CL values could be predicted from the corresponding adult values by applying AS0.75. They found that the prediction error could be especially high in the youngest children, suggesting that the use of AS0.75 is inappropriate and may introduce biased CL prediction, which cannot be explained by maturation, as maturation was not present in the model used to generate the simulated paediatric CL values. As a result, the estimated maturation function, and/or other estimated correction factors for organ function, will not only reflect maturation or organ function but also correct this introduced bias.

Strougo et al. investigated whether the maturation function in the context of AS0.75 represents maturation of enzyme activity for hepatically metabolised drugs [100]. They found that the maturation function estimated after inclusion of AS0.75 is not always interchangeable with maturation functions for the enzymes responsible for metabolising a drug, especially for children aged < 1 year. They conclude that the maturation function simultaneously accounts for enzyme maturation and other maturational changes, making the biological interpretation of the maturation function complex and therefore the between-compound extrapolation of this function restricted to very specific circumstances only. As such, they conclude that the maturation function used in combination with AS0.75 cannot be interpreted to represent enzyme maturation. As pointed out by Mahmood [101], the maturation function is also not informative regarding the overall maturation of drug CL, as MATCL50 in Eq. 7 does not capture the age at which 50% of the mature clearance value is reached, but rather the age at which half the CL obtained after AS0.75 scaling is reached.

Another limitation of the proposed maturation function is that it is unidirectional, whereas bidirectional deviations from the 3/4 allometric line have been reported [102, 103]. This is in line with the observation that, for some drugs such as warfarin, the prescribed dose per kilogram bodyweight required for the same drug exposure is higher in children aged around 2–5 years than in adults.

sec.title: Alternative Allometric Approaches to Describe Clearance in Children
sec.p: Correlations between drug CL and bodyweight and/or age are commonly high throughout childhood and do need to be accounted for. Generally, bodyweight is found to be a better descriptor than age, and it is often found that allometric exponents in estimated functions are higher than 1 at young ages and lower than 1 at older ages. This latter observation has led to the proposal of age-dependent exponents. This uses different, yet still predefined and drug-independent, allometric exponents in different ages (e.g., b = 1.2 for 0–3 months, 1.0 for 3 months–2 years, and 0.9 for > 2 years) [58, 69].

where k0, kmax, γ, k50, L, and M are estimated parameters. These BDE functions can account for the necessary asymptotic CL values at the higher extreme of the bodyweight range, as well as for bidirectional deviations from this line at lower bodyweights and the quick exponential increase in CL seen in the very young. Moreover, it gives rise to a continuous function [106], whereas age-dependent exponents yield discontinuities. Similar to the maturation function that is sometimes added to AS0.75, the number of parameters (two to four) that need to be estimated in this function do come with a requirement of a sufficiently large amount of data.

In line with the empiric nature of population pharmacokinetic models, the obtained descriptive covariate functions do not allow for biological interpretation or extrapolation outside studied covariate ranges, because all they do is quantify correlations. Therefore, the level of biological interpretability and extrapolation potential for empiric functions obtained in a data-driven approach is comparable to the maturation function of AS0.75. As such, one could wonder where the added benefit lies in introducing the debated AS0.75 function and subsequently relying on empiric elements for describing data, rather than reverting to empiric approaches from the start. If biological interpretation and extrapolation are required, other approaches such as PBPK models should ideally be employed.

sec.title: Scaling CL in Individuals with Obesity
sec.p: At the upper extreme of the human bodyweight range we find individuals with obesity, a group that is posing increasing challenges in defining drug-dosing regimens. Therefore, describing or predicting CL in individuals with obesity is receiving increased attention. Also, AS0.75 is sometimes used in this context, both to make predictions in the absence of data or for a priori inclusion in the analysis of data. However, empiric approaches have shown that CL of drugs in the obese population may increase as a function of bodyweight, or even decrease compared with normal-weight adults [107]. Additionally, around 30% of drugs show similar instead of increased CL in patients with (morbid) obesity and in normal-weight patients [107–109]. This is reflected in the values for the allometric exponent, with studies showing this exponent to vary greatly between drugs when scaling from normal-weight adults to adults with obesity, highlighting the inadequacy of the a priori selection of AS0.75 for scaling to obese individuals [110].

sec.title: Alternative Size Descriptors
sec.p: To account for the various patterns seen in CL in patients with obesity, the use of alternative body size descriptors has been proposed to replace bodyweight in the application of AS0.75. The need for different size descriptors in this population is supported by the notion that, in individuals with obesity, increases in bodyweight are driven by increases in fat mass, but because adipose tissue is not “pharmacokinetically active” it is thought not to contribute to CL [1, 91]. In this reasoning, the assumption of similarity between metabolic processes throughout the entire body (BMR) and drug CL seems to be relaxed, so where it was previously considered to be a natural extension that allometric theory for BMR is appropriate for drug elimination clearance in specific organs, in the context of obesity these concepts are now explained to be limited to specific tissues only. Others pointed out that, because the body composition of individuals with obesity is significantly different from that of non-obese individuals, bodyweight would be a descriptor of both size and shape. As allometric theory is a study of size only, other size descriptors are needed [111].

Here, Ffat is estimated from data, which again adds empiric elements to the theoretical framework. Similarly to the maturation function in children, this is required to allow reconciliation of theory with observations. However, in a large meta-analysis of 121 pharmacokinetic models in adults, McLeay et al. found that not one of these descriptors outperformed the others, whereas lean bodyweight with an exponent of 2/3 performed best on average [66], which is in line with findings of others [114, 117].

sec.title: Theoretical Critiques on the Alternative Size Descriptors
sec.p: Empirically, comparative studies of the descriptive properties of the different size descriptors indeed suggest that there is not one single descriptor that is most appropriate for all drugs [107]. This challenges the universality of AS0.75 and its derived extensions in individuals with obesity and suggests that application of data-driven techniques per individual drug may be most appropriate. Some authors have suggested that elimination routes are predictive as drivers of changes in CL with obesity, but this has also been rejected [107], because other drug properties such as the extraction ratio and fraction unbound also drive drug CL. Finally, other aspects such as changes in the expression of drug transporters can influence the observed CL in individuals with obesity, whereas the metabolic processes themselves remain unchanged [118].

In addition to the theoretical aspects of this discussion, it has been pointed out that individuals with obesity may have a range of comorbidities, which may impact drug CL further. Additionally, the duration of obesity may impact drug CL. For example, renal function can increase with obesity but, over time, renal function may decrease because of kidney damage. Within the framework of AS0.75, this can be accounted for by the inclusion of additional covariates; however, particularly when comorbidities are correlated with the degree of obesity, similar issues with biological interpretation of these estimated functions arise as with the interpretation of the maturation function in the paediatric population.

sec.title: Lack of Universality of the Allometric Exponent in Pharmacology Across Varying Drug Properties
sec.p: As for BMR, also for drug CL, claims of a lack of a unique and universal allometric exponent are increasing, although the arguments differ. The essence of the discussion on CL revolves around drug properties. An important variable underlying drug CL is intrinsic activity of drug metabolising enzymes and/or drug transporters, which is driven in part by the size of the liver and kidneys, but hepatic or renal blood flow, unbound drug fraction, and blood-to-plasma ratio also impact drug CL. The impact on drug CL of changes in these variables depends on the properties of the drug, for which the extraction ratio is an important determinant. Drugs with a high extraction ratio are predominantly sensitive to changes in organ blood flow, whereas drugs with a low extraction ratio are more sensitive to changes in the other variables, with unbound drug fraction and blood-to-plasma ratio being subjected to changes in plasma protein binding and partitioning into red blood cells or to changes in the concentration of drug binding plasma proteins or the haematocrit. In children and individuals with obesity, changes in bodyweight will lead to changes in organ size and blood flow according to distinctly different non-linear functions, which may even cause the extraction ratio to change with age or obesity [119]. As such, it can come as no surprise that changes in drug CL must follow different patterns for drugs with differing properties. In addition to these size-related changes, age in children, and body mass index in individuals with obesity are correlated with changes in the expression and/or activity of enzymes and transporters per gram of eliminating organ, in the expression of drug-binding plasma proteins, and haematocrit [99, 120], which will have an additional impact on the CL of drugs that differs for drugs with different properties.

Understanding these concepts explains differences in empiric findings, because as the ‘true’ allometric exponent will depend on drug properties, specific allometric scaling exponents may become more or less appropriate depending on the drug being investigated. The availability of PBPK approaches that are considered gold standard, particularly for the paediatric population [121–123], have provided an opportunity to establish a priori what drugs and in what scenarios AS0.75 or other scaling approaches lead to sufficiently accurate CL predictions in both paediatrics and individuals with obesity [117, 124]. It is important to keep in mind that these analyses do not provide support for the theoretical basis of a specific approach, rather they provide an overview of the cases in which its pragmatic application is accurate.

sec.title: Practical Considerations for Applying AS0.75 in Human Pharmacology
sec.p:
From this overview, it appears that discussions within the field of ecology are mirrored in the pharmacological arena. In both fields, there are those who have absolute faith in allometric theory, who are diametrically opposed by those unconvinced of the theoretical basis. In the end, the opponents reject the idea of a universal scaling exponent in favour of an exponent that is variable depending on the interplay of many variables. Ecologists cite evolutionary reasons; pharmacologists highlight the interplay of physiological processes with drugs of differing physicochemical properties. Moreover, it can be questioned whether the proposed extensions of AS0.75 in human pharmacology, as illustrated in Fig. 5, still align with the original theory and with the promise of ease and universality, or whether they are mere necessities to reconcile theory with observations. Aside from these theoretical considerations, some practical aspects for the use of AS0.75 must be considered.Fig. 5

The green lines represent clinically observed patterns, with (1) in the very young clearance values that are below the allometric line, (2) in children between approximately 2 and 5 years clearance values above the allometric line, and (3) a wide range of patterns in the obese population with clearance values increasing, decreasing, or remaining constant with increasing bodyweight. sec.title: Do We Have Power to Estimate the Exponent, and Does It Matter?
sec.p: In many studies, the allometric exponent is estimated instead of fixed. The most common argument against estimation of the exponent is that study designs commonly lack the power to accurately estimate this exponent. Interestingly, in this context, there seems less worry about the power of studies to estimate maturation functions using PMA or PNA as a covariate, or to estimate correction factors for obesity (Ffat) or disease as part of the AS0.75 scaling approach, or to identify the most appropriate size descriptor. Moreover, when exponent values close to 0.75 are obtained in data-driven analyses (or if it is included in the 95% confidence interval), the obtained value is considered trustworthy enough by some to be used as an argument to support AS0.75 [1, 125, 126].

Indeed, a number of publications show that, when AS0.75 is used to simulate concentration–time data from common study designs, a range in exponent values is found when re-estimating the exponent based on the simulated data [1, 127] and that this can lead to differences in predicted drug exposure ranging from − 51 to + 90% [128]. Although these reports confirm important limitations of study designs that should be addressed, they do not prove the appropriateness or universality of AS0.75. If the other exponents were used in simulations and AS0.75 were used in re-estimation, similar degrees of bias would inevitably be found. So, although simulation and re-estimation techniques can be used to assess whether a study design provides data that yield identifiability of model features and parameters, they cannot be used to support or reject the theoretical basis of the model selected in the simulation phase.

Discussions on the value of the allometric exponent often overlook that the CL values obtained with a covariate function, instead of the allometric exponent, are of primary interest. A number of publications have shown that, between 25 and 90 kg, allometric exponents below 1 will all yield very similar relationships between bodyweight and CL [127, 129], which suggests that bias in the allometric exponent may lead to only limited bias in CL [99, 124, 127]. This lack of sensitivity to the value of the exponent will reduce the power to estimate the value of the exponent and diminish the importance of a precise estimate of the exponent in describing the allometric relationship for drug CL. As exemplified by Fischer et al., the theoretical differences in CL estimations between a weight-proportional and allometric model are overshadowed and rendered insignificant by the unexplained inter-individual variability present in an actual data set [129]. Overall, these studies show that there is not one clear advantage of using a certain exponent and that, in many cases, it may not matter much altogether. From this, it can also be concluded that the success of AS0.75 in describing CL in children aged > 5 years is not a testament to the solid theoretical basis but can rather be attributable to the lack of sensitivity of CL values to the allometric exponent in this age and weight range.

sec.title: Importance of Model Evaluation
sec.p: Regardless of what covariate relationship is included in a population model, descriptive properties of the model and therefore the appropriateness of clinical interpretations derived from model findings, need to be confirmed in suitable model evaluation techniques. The use of model-based simulations, for instance to establish individualised dosing guidelines, also require assessment of the model’s predictive performance. Different techniques provide different information regarding the robustness of obtained parameter values, covariate relationships, and model performance; therefore, multiple techniques are required in conjunction. Moreover, certain features common for data obtained in special populations may require specific attention, as exemplified by Krekels et al. for the paediatric population [98].

To assess predictive model properties, focus should be on population predictions, rather than individual predictions, as misspecification in the structural model can be corrected by individual eta values, which may lead to unbiased individual predictions in the presence of structural misspecification and biased population predictions [98]. Particularly when assessing any allometric relationship for CL, it is highly important to plot eta values for CL versus bodyweight to ascertain that trends are appropriately captured. When the data of the (special) population contain covariates that are correlated with bodyweight (e.g., age in children), the eta values should also be plotted against this covariate. Stratification of various validation plots, including goodness-of-fit plots based on weight strata, is also useful. Simulation-based diagnostics assess the predictive properties of models. For this purpose, the visual predictive check (VPC) is often advocated, partly because of its ease of interpretation. However, in the presence of a highly variable dosing regimen, often observed in studies that are performed during routine clinical practice or that involve dose titration, or in the presence of (multiple) continuous covariates, this method becomes increasingly inappropriate, which is not fully addressed by proposed adaptations (e.g., prediction-corrected VPC) that also diminish the ease of interpretation [98]. In this context, normalised prediction distribution errors [130] assess the same performance feature as the VPC, while being always methodologically appropriate and offering both visual and statistical outcomes for model assessment.

sec.p:

sec.title: Conclusions and Perspectives
sec.p:
The benefit of theories is ease and universality of use. This promise may be why allometric theories are so strongly sought and defended, but the substantial evidence undermining the theoretical basis of AS0.75 in (human) pharmacology cannot be denied. Looking back at Fig. 4 (right panel), we conclude that the foundation is unsupported and that the assumptions that form the pillars to support use of AS0.75 in human pharmacology do not hold, for the following reasons.
The initial observation of an allometric exponent of 3/4 by Kleiber has been refuted. Other studies have concluded, even based on the same data as Kleiber, that an allometric exponent of 2/3 cannot be rejected for mammals < 10 kg and birds [35], that the exponent changes over the bodyweight range [9, 35, 44, 46, 47], and that the obtained exponent is highly dependent on the selected species in Kleiber’s dataset [8, 41, 46].
The existence of a single, universal allometric scaling exponent is highly debated, and the exponent has been proposed to be variable in nature [54].
WBE1997 offer one possible explanation for an allometric exponent of 3/4 but no proof that this must be the case. Moreover, the framework relies on multiple assumptions that have been critiqued based on theoretical arguments, mathematical derivations, and empirical observations, as summarised in Table 1.
Not a single argument or theoretical support is provided for the assertion that the same principles would apply to drug CL as to BMR. WBE1997 is often cited as support for this statement, but it is difficult to reconcile the assumptions in WBE1997 with the physiology of CL processes.
There is no support for the extension of between-species theoretical allometric scaling to within-species allometric scaling. Empirically, evidence does not support this for BMR [43, 44]. In human pharmacology, it is only possible to reconcile the theory with observations after extensions of the AS0.75 framework that are summarised in Fig. 5 but that have been questioned by others. PBPK principles show that there cannot be one universal allometric scaling exponent for CL for all drugs because changes in CL are the result of a complex interplay between drug-specific and system-specific parameters. As such, it stands to reason that a ‘Darwinian view’ of allometric scaling proposed by Glazier for BMR is also applicable to the field of pharmacology.

Despite these arguments, AS0.75 may hold empirical merit in human pharmacology (Table 2), as this approach has been shown to lead to accurate descriptions of the correlation between bodyweight and CL for children as young as 5 years of age [99]. However, it is important to note that this is not the case for children aged < 5 years or for children with obesity or malnutrition. It must also be reiterated that AS0.75, and maturation or organ functions estimated in conjunction with it, have no biological meaning and cannot be used for biological interpretations or extrapolations. Additionally, incidental successes of AS0.75 cannot be used to substantiate allometric theory in its entirety. Stern belief in theory, but disregard of the theoretical weakness, overshadows empirical merit as conclusions are drawn on disputed presumptions. Empirical merit also comes with a prerequisite of appropriate model evaluation to support model findings, because even when the chosen methodology can remain a point of debate, empirical merit is ultimately proven in model validation.
